newsitem.title: CHINA: Seoul, Pyongyang Red Cross resume food aid talks.
newsitem.headline: Seoul, Pyongyang Red Cross resume food aid talks.

text.p: The Red Cross societies of South and North Korea resumed talks in Beijing on Monday aimed at speeding up food aid to the hungry and isolated North.
A first session of talks, the first inter-Korean Red Cross talks in almost five years, was held in the Chinese capital last Friday. Officials could not say how long the talks would continue.
Lee Byung-woong, secretary general of South Korea's Red Cross, said on Friday he expected good results when the talks resumed on Monday.

The North is sliding into famine after the Stalinist hermit nation was hit by devastating floods in 1995 and 1996, with officials reporting deaths of children from malnutrition and farmers eating sawdust to fill out their diet.
At the talks last week, the South said it wanted to secure fast and efficient delivery of food aid to the North to cut costs and delivery time. Officials have declined to give details.
Red Cross officials say the talks would focus on procedures for transporting and distributing food for the North, but not the size or timing of aid.

Red Cross officials in Seoul have said South Korea would propose delivering food aid through the Korean border village of Panmunjom, instead of the present methods of using ships or trains through China.
The South also wanted to hand over aid directly to the North instead of through the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, Red Cross officials in Seoul said.
North Korea has said its food supplies would run out at the end of April.
The U.N. World Food Programme estimated there was enough food to feed the country only until June and then its 24 million people would have to wait for the next harvest in October and November.
South Korea, the United States and Japan are scheduled to hold talks in Tokyo on May 7 to discuss food shortages in the North and ways to encourage Pyongyang to join peace talks.
Seoul, Washington and Tokyo are worried that a desperate North Korean leadership might strike the South if an economic crisis threatened its survival.
Peace talks have been proposed involving the two Koreas, the United States and China, to try to close the book on the 1950-53 Korean War, which ended in a now-fraying armistice.
North Korea last month agreed to join the four-nation peace talks if it was first guaranteed large-scale food aid, U.S. diplomatic recognition and an easing of trade sanctions.
The United States has pledged $25 million and South Korea $6 million to the World Food Programme, which has appealed for $95.5 million to provide 203,000 tonnes of food to North Korea.
South Korea has said it was considering sending an additional 50,000 tonnes of corn.

Japan has held back food aid, partly due to anger over charges that North Korea kidnapped a Japanese schoolgirl in 1977 and spirited her to Pyongyang. The United States has said it would not press Japan to donate more food aid to North Korea.
